series: Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.4 · October 2026
title: Are CPAT's Price Elasticities Right?

slides.title: Are CPAT's Price Elasticities Right?
slides.subtitle: A check of the Climate Policy Assessment Tool's defaults against the evidence
slides.message: Most defaults are consistent with the evidence and many are cautious; two are too high. The bigger problem is timing: CPAT applies in the first year a response that takes a decade, so near-term cuts are overstated by about half.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity

slides.title: Price elasticities decide the size of CPAT's answers

stats.label: cut in G20 CO₂ by 2030 from a carbon tax rising to $75/t, with CPAT's default elasticities
the same cut with every elasticity moved two standard deviations down or up
an elasticity twice the true value doubles the estimated cut and the speed the tax base erodes

slides.text: No other parameter in CPAT's sensitivity tests moves the result as much. The defaults were calibrated to one meta-analysis and checked mainly against their own targets.
slides.source: CPAT documentation, Parameter Sensitivity Analysis (CPAT-AI repository); Brief 5.3.

slides.title: The two failures come from stretching thin sector evidence across fuels
slides.note: Sector adjustments estimated over all fuels were applied to fuels with almost no sector studies; CPAT's own panel study flagged both.
slides.source: CPAT defaults for developing countries; working paper 5.4, Table 1. Medians exclude CPAT's calibration source.

slides.title: For road fuels, the published averages themselves overstate the response

stats.label: long-run gasoline elasticity before and after correcting for publication bias
long-run gasoline elasticity in 32 fuel-subsidizing economies
CPAT's road gasoline value for developing countries: twice the corrected mean

slides.text: Journals publish large, significant estimates more readily. Tax salience pulls the other way (in Sweden the carbon-tax elasticity was three times the price elasticity), so show a low-elasticity case beside the central result rather than cutting the defaults.
slides.source: Havranek, Irsova and Janda (2012); Arzaghi and Squalli (2015); Andersson (2019).

slides.title: CPAT applies in year one a response that takes a decade
slides.caption: Own-price elasticity by years after a permanent price rise: CPAT (dashed) against gradual adjustment (solid; bands: other speeds).

points.lead: Use adjusts in a year or two;
points.text: equipment only as it wears out: cars about 7% a year, buildings 1–2%.
about a fifth of CPAT's response has happened; after five, about 60%.
list the missing short-run response as a known issue.

slides.source: Author's calculation; Black et al. (2022), Annex C; CPAT Technical Notes (2022), section 3.1.8.6.

slides.title: Five years out, CPAT overstates the response by about half, and by up to double
slides.note: Early cuts are overstated and early carbon-tax revenue understated; for subsidy reform, the fall in consumption arrives too early. Phasing prices in reduces the error but does not remove it.
slides.source: Author's calculation, working paper 5.4, Table 3. Central speeds: use 30% a year, equipment 6.7% a year; alternatives: use within the year, equipment 2% a year.
